# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease [1]. First described in detail by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the condition was initially regarded as a curiosity but has since been recognized as a clinically relevant cause of recurrent chest pain and adverse cardiac events [2]. Despite decades of investigation, the pathophysiology remains incompletely understood, and management is largely empirical [3].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is most commonly quantified using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count, a reproducible objective method introduced by Gibson and colleagues [4]. A corrected TIMI frame count exceeding two standard deviations above the normal mean for a given vessel defines slow flow [5]. The phenomenon must be distinguished from the no-reflow phenomenon, which typically occurs after percutaneous coronary intervention or acute myocardial infarction [6]. CSFP frequently involves multiple vessels, although the left anterior descending artery is often the most affected because of its length [7].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is observed in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [8]. It is more prevalent in young and middle-aged men, particularly smokers, and is frequently associated with metabolic disturbances [9]. Many affected patients present with recurrent rest angina, and a substantial proportion require repeated hospital admissions [10].

## Pathophysiology

Several overlapping mechanisms have been proposed. Microvascular dysfunction is the most widely supported hypothesis, supported by findings of elevated microvascular resistance and abnormal coronary flow reserve [11]. Endothelial dysfunction, evidenced by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilation, is consistently demonstrated in CSFP cohorts [12]. Histopathological studies of patients with CSFP have revealed myointimal proliferation, medial hypertrophy, and small-vessel fibromuscular changes [13]. Subclinical diffuse atherosclerosis detectable by intravascular ultrasound, even in angiographically smooth vessels, has also been implicated [14].

Inflammation appears central to the process. Elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and other inflammatory markers have been reported [15]. Oxidative stress, with increased markers such as malondialdehyde and reduced antioxidant capacity, contributes to endothelial injury [16]. Platelet activation and increased mean platelet volume suggest a prothrombotic milieu [17]. Disturbances in nitric oxide and endothelin-1 balance favor a vasoconstrictive state [18].

## Clinical Associations and Risk Factors

CSFP has been linked to insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and abnormal lipid profiles [19]. Increased epicardial adipose tissue and obesity are recognized correlates [20]. Hyperuricemia and elevated homocysteine levels have likewise been associated with the phenomenon [21]. Several reports have described an association with atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, including increased P-wave and QT dispersion, which may explain reports of syncope and, rarely, sudden cardiac death [22].

## Clinical Presentation and Prognosis

The dominant clinical manifestation is recurrent angina, which may occur at rest and can mimic acute coronary syndromes [23]. Although historically considered benign, longitudinal data indicate that CSFP carries a measurable burden of recurrent symptoms, impaired quality of life, and occasional major adverse cardiovascular events [24]. Acute presentations, including non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and ventricular tachyarrhythmia, have been documented [25].

## Management

No guideline-endorsed therapy exists, and treatment is directed at symptoms and underlying mechanisms [26]. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as mibefradil and diltiazem, have shown benefit in improving TIMI frame counts and reducing angina [27]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric oxide–potentiating properties, has demonstrated improvement in endothelial function and flow parameters [28]. Dipyridamole and other agents targeting microvascular tone have been explored with variable results [29]. Statins and lifestyle modification, including smoking cessation and management of metabolic risk factors, are recommended given the inflammatory and endothelial contributions [30].

## Conclusion

The coronary slow flow phenomenon is a distinct angiographic and clinical entity that reflects a complex interplay of microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, inflammation, and subclinical atherosclerosis. Although often labeled benign, it imposes a meaningful symptom burden and may be associated with arrhythmic and ischemic complications. The TIMI frame count provides a simple, reproducible diagnostic tool. Future research should focus on standardizing diagnostic thresholds, clarifying mechanisms, and establishing evidence-based therapeutic strategies through adequately powered randomized trials.
